title: Out of the depths (Psalm 130)
hook: my soul waits more than watchmen for the morning

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dreamers of the Negev, and a farmer planting through tears. Your line was sow in tears, reap in joy. What small hopeful thing did you plant? Day four hundred thirty-five.

Four in the morning on a city wall. The watchman has been up since midnight. His eyes ache. The torches are low. Every shadow in the valley could be an enemy, and it's his job to see it first. Nothing to do but stand there and look east. He knows morning will come. It always has. But knowing doesn't make the last hour shorter. He watches the sky for the first thin gray line along the hills, the sign that he can finally go home and sleep. Anyone who has worked a night shift, sat up with a sick child, or waited for a phone call knows that hour. Today's psalm lives there.
screen: `FOUR A.M. ON THE WALL.` → `EYES ON THE EAST.` → `THE LONGEST HOUR.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred thirty is short, eight verses, and it begins at the bottom. In the King James Bible: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD." Depths is the word for deep water, the kind you go under. In Latin the psalm is known by its first words, De profundis. Then comes a startling question: "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" If God kept a record of every wrong, nobody would be left on their feet. The answer comes straight away: "But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared." Not a God with a ledger. A God with forgiveness, which makes him worth revering. Then the waiting. "I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning." He says it twice. You can feel the hour dragging. And then, in the last two verses, the psalmist turns from himself to his whole people: let Israel hope, for with the Lord there is mercy, and plenteous redemption. Christians have long counted this among the seven penitential psalms, prayers of turning back. Martin Luther made it a hymn. Catholics pray the De profundis for the dead, and it is sung at evening prayer. It's also another song of going up, from the pilgrims' collection. Which means the people who sang it out of the depths were walking uphill as they sang.
screen: `DE PROFUNDIS: OUT OF THE DEPTHS` · `NOT A LEDGER, BUT FORGIVENESS` · `MORE THAN WATCHMEN FOR MORNING` · `FROM ONE VOICE TO A PEOPLE` · then, large: `MY SOUL WAITETH FOR THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait for one thing with hope. Sit, and let your body settle. Name to yourself one thing you're waiting for. A result, a reconciliation, a change in someone you love, a morning after a long night. Hold it the way the watchman holds the horizon: not grabbing, not giving up. Eyes on the east. Breathe slowly. Each breath out is one more minute closer to the light. If you pray, you can say: my soul waiteth for the Lord. If you don't, simply wait, hoping, without demanding when. The bell holds the time.
De profundis. Latin for out of the depths, Psalm one hundred thirty's cry from deep water, and a soul waiting for God more than watchmen wait for morning.
Your line: more than watchmen for morning. Today, if you're waiting on something hard, watch for one first sign of light, however small, and name it when it comes. Day four hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Psalm 130 is one of the seven penitential psalms; Catholics traditionally pray the De profundis for the dead, many churches sing it at evening prayer and funerals, and Lutherans sing Luther's hymn version.
